speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the critical atmosphere of doubt and uncertainty created by the conflicting statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), the Premier of Quebec and the Mayor of Montreal regarding the nature of the threat to the democratically elected government of Quebec and the administration of Montreal which led the government to proclaim the War Measures Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 NATIONAL SECURITY INFORMATION LEADING TO INVOKING OF WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for York South has filed the notice prescribed under Standing Order 26. His proposed motion deals with a matter which is, of course, of extreme importance. Because the application of the War Measures Act has such far-reaching effects on individual freedom, the matter has to be of prime concern to Parliament. This is why very special care must be taken to ensure that all reasonable opportunities for debate must be afforded.
In this regard, it will be noted that the exhaustive and earnest debate which took place in the House following the proclamation of the Act has provided one such opportunity. Since then, debate on the Speech from the Throne has continued and has given hon. members further occasions to consider the many aspects of the matter. In
addition, the daily question period has been concerned principally with the situation created by the proclamation of the War Measures Act.
The fact that these opportunities have been provided by ordinary daily procedures does not mean that a special debate might not be held under the terms of Standing Order 26. I suggest to hon. members that while this may be very useful the Chair cannot overlook the provision in the Standing Orders that in a given session there can only be one debate about a particular matter. If we are to have at any time an emergency debate I would think that hon. members would want the Chair to exercise extreme caution in selecting the circumstances under which such debate should be undertaken.
The motion proposed by the hon. member focuses on suggested discrepancies between ministerial statements dealing with the circumstances which have preceded proclamation of the Act. The hon. member charges that these statements have resulted in what he terms a "critical atmosphere of doubt and uncertainty". To my mind, the proposed motion is more in the nature of a censure motion which might well be presented to the House by other procedures.
Standing Order 26 and the practice which has evolved in the application of the Standing Order require that the Chair should take into consideration the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means. The Minister of Justice has indicated to the House that legislation to be substituted for the regulations under the War Measures Act will be introduced soon. Of course, I cannot commit the minister to any timetable, but my interpretation of an answer he gave earlier this week is that the legislation will be introduced next week.
In the circumstances, and taking into account the relevant procedural requirements set out in Standing Order 26 and in our practice, I must come to the conclusion that the hon. member's motion cannot be put.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question, which enables me to shed some light on the matter. First of all, I will say that the answer given in the House the other day was correct and that it is based on Section 227 of the National Defence Act. I did say that the cost of these

services will be paid by the province which asked for the intervention of the armed forces. The reason for this is that when members of the armed forces go to a province at the request of the attorney general of that province, they act as peace officers not as soldiers. Right now they are not in Quebec under the orders of Canada's commander in chief but under those of the provincial authorities and I think that this is what the people of Quebec want, that is to have the initiative of maintaining peace in their own province. The federal government is certainly not going to get involved in this aspect of their business.
Given the foregoing, I must point out that the regulations adopted under this legislation provide that only additional expenditures must be paid by the province which requested the services of the armed forces. In other words, the province will not be required to assume the costs of the soldier's regular pay or rations, only the extra expenses incurred as a result of provincial authorities requesting the members of the armed forces to do this additional work.
If I may continue, Mr. Speaker. It might be better for me to wait for supplementary questions and I hope there will be some.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the hon. member that when the city of Montreal asked the armed forces to intervene last year, the request was made by the Attorney General of the province of Quebec and Quebec authorities paid for the additional work done by the armed forces.
I could further say that whenever armed forces are sent to other provinces to bring assistance in cases of flood, for instance, although the situation is not exactly the same, the federal government usually sends the bill to the provincial authorities concerned.
This being so, Mr. Speaker, it is true that 12 hours after the province of Quebec had asked for the support of the armed forces-and this for the first time in peacetime-the War Measures Act was enforced. It is therefore possible that from thereon, it should be necessary to make other arrangements for that payment. I have already spoken to Premier Bourassa to that effect. I told him that we should settle the matter together. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: APPREHENDED INSURRECTION-REPORTED SUPPLYING OF ADDITIONAL INFORMATION TO LIBERAL MEMBERS

speechtext: Well, for a very simple reason, Mr. Speaker. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION TO JUNE 30, 1973
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel some obligation to speak on Bill C-4 because I come from an area to which the provisions of this act apply.
The bill under study is entitled "An Act to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act", and is introduced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene). It contains the following recommendation:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House the present measure to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Act to extend its application to June 30, 1973.
This new bill proposes four changes which, on the whole, merely authorize an extension of the assistance to gold mines up to June 30, 1973. The first change provides for an extension of the application of the act until 1973; the second provides for an increase of 25 per cent in assistance.
According to clause 2 of the bill, this Act will not apply to mines that were not in production during the month immediately preceding August 7, 1970.
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
Mr. Speaker, there may be reasons why certain mines did not produce during the month preceding August 7, 1970. Perhaps they did not because they had not received enough assistance to produce or maintain their operations. The explanatory notes of clause 3 are as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to require a person who receives any payment under the act to agree to hire any new employees through the facilities of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, to give four months' notice of the closing of his mine to the minister-
This is a rather important clause because, not so long ago, we witnessed the closing of a mine in the area of Cadillac. No notice had then been given and hundreds of workers were laid off without anyone guaranteeing them any security whatsoever or helping them in any way to find other employment.
And mining authorities of the province of Quebec are still faced with the problem of the Cadillac-Molly mine that closed its doors without notice.
I continue quoting the explanatory notes for clause 3:
-and to use the services of the Department of Manpower and Immigration for the purposes of finding employment for the former employees.
Mr. Speaker, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act adopted in 1948 seeked to help gold mine operators to overcome economic difficulties caused by increased production costs and a stable gold price. The purpose of this legislation was to extend gold mining operations and to give people in communities where their living depends on such operations a chance to gradually adapt themselves to the reduction of financial support.
An amendment to the legislation in 1967, that is 19 years later, extended its enforcement for a 3-year period, that is up to December 31, 1970.
The number of reef mines eligible for assistance provided by the legislation has decreased from 87 in 1948, to 44 in 1960 and to 35 in 1968.
Five reef mines which received financial assistance provided by the legislation put an end to their operations in 1968 and it is expected that four or five others will do the same before the end of 1971, if they do not receive any assistance.
The Wasamac mine No. 2 in the Rouyn-Noranda area remained the only mine in operation in 1968.
The amounts paid to gold mine operators as of March 31, 1969, for the years 1948 to 1968 inclusive amounted to $261,293,250.09 for a production of 57,166,704 ounces of gold sold in accordance with the provisions of the legislation.
The total amount of assistance payable for gold produced and sold during the calendar year 1968 is estimated at $14,300,000. As of March 31, 1969, the total assistance paid for 1968 amounted to $11,430,163.02, that is about 90 per cent of the assistance granted as a result of applications already received. The remainder is payable following an audit of the applicants' books.
I have here a table showing the amounts of assistance paid from 1948 to 1968 to all the gold mines in operation in Canada. I also have a table which shows the produc-
744
October 30, 1970

Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
tion of bullion in Canada from 1948 to 1968. For the year 1968 I can see a production of 2,748,333 ounces of gold.
In northwestern Quebec, the Horne mine was to prove the richest in Canada. This discovery was but the first of several others which helped make this mining area the most important in all the province of Quebec for a good number of years.
From 1922 on, the Noranda Company has developped into a major concern and is today an internationally known company which has the facilities here in Quebec to process copper ore and to manufacture finished products.
The operation of the Horne mine opened the way for the Noranda foundry-the biggest in the world-and later for the Canadian Copper Refiners plant in Montreal East, the most important copper refinery in the world.
Since the first delivery made by the Horne mine to the Noranda foundry, 54 million tons of ore have been extracted from that vein and this ore has produced nearly 1,200,000 tons of copper and 8,300,000 ounces of gold. In 1967 the production of that operation amounted to $24 million. The foundry of the Horne complex has handled since the beginning more than 17 million tons of copper concentrates originating from other Quebec mines and other provinces. In 1967 the deliveries of the foundry amounted to $227 million. The Horne complex, including the mine, the concentrator and the foundry, provides 1,600 jobs and pays each year $9.5 million in salaries.
The Noranda Mines Company reinvested a part of the profits in the exploration of the area in the immediate vicinity of Noranda and of the whole territory of the province. With the years, this company discovered or acquired a participation in several concerns already existing in Quebec, as for example, the Quemont mine which has been working for 20 years a copper-zinc-gold-silver-pyrite deposit. This concern has extracted, since the beginning of its operations, 14 million tons of ore; it employs 350 persons and pays each year $2.5 million in salaries.
The situation is about the same for the Normetal Mining Corporation Ltd., located some 75 miles north of Noranda, near the Ontario border.
The Noranda group, although it is dominant is not the only one active in the area: Lake Dufault Mines Ltd., a branch of Falconbridge, has been operating since 1964 a copper-tin-gold-silver lode which, although of limited size, has contributed more than $75 million to Quebec mineral production. In 1968, metal deliveries reached $13 million and some 250 persons were employed.
Wasamac mines operate two small gold lodes in the Noranda area; one since 1965 and the other since May 1968.
The ore treated at the Noranda foundry is routed to Canadian Copper Refiners in Montreal East, which supply work for 1400 persons, whose salaries total $9,000,000 a year. Moreover, each year, more than $8 million are earmarked for the purchase of materials and supplies. Part of this refinery production supplies in turn the
Noranda Copper Mills plant built in Montreal East in 1942. The latter employs 950 people and pays salaries that amount to $6.8 million.
On the other hand, the mining industry in Noranda gave rise on the site to related industries, such as Quebec Iron Foundries, a plant that manufactures crushing agents used mainly during the first phase of ore processing. Quebec Iron Foundries owns a chain of foundries throughout Canada, two of which in Quebec, one in Noranda and the other in Mont-Joli.
Those are but a few examples of the great natural resources potential to be found in our area, that is in northwestern Quebec.
Since the start of the mining industry in the Abitibi area, all levels of government have made tremendous investments to allow newcomers to live as full-fledged citizens or, at least, as close as possible to the minimum standards of the twenteth century.
In the fields of roads, education, hospitalization, social services, technical services, communications, radio, television, and so forth, local structures have been established at considerable expense to allow the Abitibi people to develop normally, at the same speed as the inhabitants of other areas; anyway, directly or indirectly, all levels of government, with the help of the Canadian taxpayers, have footed the bill.
Following such efforts and such investments, we would hate to see some municipalities turn into ghost towns because the industry which was the backbone of their economy, could no longer operate.
There is no need to cavil about the causes of the difficulties encountered by the gold mines as they are well known. Moreover the federal authorities are aware of the problem that is to be faced not only by the operators of the gold mines but also by the civic authorities, municipal councils, school boards and especially the workers directly involved in those operations.
For some years now we have been witnessing something new in our area; owners of gold mines have to close down their operations not because of a depletion of ore but because extracting costs are too high and grants too small. Such conditions are a cause of alarm to us and one must expect, should those conditions remain, that they will get worse to such a point that other industries will have to close down also.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Villeneuve (M. Tetrault) was right when he said a while ago that the government subsidizes western wheat producers for not producing any wheat but that it will not subsidize gold production at a time when we would be sure of using or exporting the whole of our gold production, while we are not sure of exporting the whole of our wheat production. Since we are not sure of being able to export our wheat, our farmers are paid for not producing and while we are sure of being able to export the whole of our gold production, payments for producing gold are being refused. To me that is an irresponsible behaviour on the part of the government and that is what my colleague from Villeneuve was pointing out a while ago when he

October 30, 1970

showed the government the foolishness of their protection measures, for not producing wheat on the one hand and not stimulating gold production on the other hand, and yet gold is a product that permits us commercial exchanges with the United States, that are ready to absorb the whole of our gold production.
Mr. Speaker, the government ought to improve greatly the assistance to gold mines. The gold producers are not asking for a handout from the government, on the contrary, they want it to encourage the development of new mines in that area, if only to meet the needs of the people.
It is therefore of vital importance to the cities in our area that the mining industry be maintained and developed.
To all those who live where gold mines are being exploited, as well as to those who from one end of the country to the other supply goods and services, that act has been a source of great benefit in the past; this is no time to repeal it nor to let it stagnate. It must be improved with a view to contributing even more to the economic development of our area, as well as that of north western Quebec and north eastern Ontario.
The act has played an important social role by protecting the family and society where gold mines are being operated. It has helped, up to a point; but it has harmed, for instance, the development of new mines.
Has any thought been given to those citizens who, after working in gold mines for 20, 25 years, and building a little house at Val-d'Or, Malartic, Noranda, Rouyn, Amos, La Sarre, or Normetal, have been forced to go into exile, to work at Thompson in northern Manitoba, or Sudbury, or in other Canadian provinces, and to leave their homes and what they own behind, in the community in which they have lived for so many years?
o (12:10p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the government is responsible for this situation. It does not have the right to tolerate, to bring about this situation as it is doing now. As I said, the act played a significant part in protecting the family, but did not fulfil this role to the extent that we could keep our fellow citizens in our area by enabling them, through some assistance, to work at the development of new mines.
Thanks to this act, many workers continued to live decently, when otherwise they would have been forced to go. Some actually had to, because the act was not generous enough. They were able to raise their children, to provide them with adequate food and clothing for 35 or 40 years, whereas had it not been for the act, they might have suffered from poverty, although they are not very rich.
Finally, thanks to that act, an important group of taxpayers-companies or individuals-have kept on paying federal, provincial and municipal taxes. Does the government, by providing assistance to gold mines, not get back a great part of the money through various taxes, hidden or official, in many different ways, such as income taxes, pension plans, etc.? The government turns again to the taxpayers for money. Consumers are left with no pur-
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
chasing power after all the governments have helped themselves to the workers' pay envelope.
Not only companies' stockholders but also a whole segment of the population live directly or indirectly off the gold mining industry.
The present policy towards laid-off workers under which part of the cost of relocating these people in other mining communities is paid, might of course have adverse effects later on other manufacturing sectors because of a drop in population. It must be realized that most miners being married and having lived in these cities for many years, it is inconceivable to claim that only the head of the family will have to move. This would mean, in short, if 100 miners were to leave, a loss of at least 500 individuals who might, in several cases, fill a position with other industries.
In a short while, other gold mines will have to shut down because of a lack of manpower and of exhorbitant operating costs. A generalisation of this situation would obviously result in a business slump that our cities will not be able to stand. It is easy, therefore, to foresee the slow but certain disappearance of all other industries.
Considering the present needs and the new commitments to be assumed in a changing society which requires more public services, particularly in education, we think it is the right time to adjust the grants to gold mines to enable the management-and that is one of the main objects-to give their employees wage increases similar to those granted in other industrial sectors.
I am urgently asking that those who work in gold mines get the same treatment as those who are employed in other mines or industries. Today, there is an obvious difference between the salaries paid to gold miners and those paid to workers in other industries.
Despite the considerable mechanization which contributed to ease the inflationary pressures on costs through manpower reduction, the mining industry has always depended on a significant human participation. Wages make up from 55 to 60 per cent of production costs. Therefore, the mining industry provides openings for the labour force.
Each dollar of assistance protects about $5 in salary and $2 in supplies obtained from different localities in Canada. That consequence, in human terms, has some importance.
The firms and the men who keep on working, thanks mainly to the act, have paid back to the federal government, in the form of taxes, almost 50 per cent of the aid received, including sales taxes, and even close to 75 per cent, if taxation at all levels of government is taken into account.
On behalf of a worried population who wants to save whatever can still be saved, not only in order to maintain the production of gold, but to promote a certain development of that industry, so that other mines may begin production, if their owners have the certainty that the operation is at least a profitable venture, the urgency of such an act providing for assistance to the operation of gold mines leaves no doubt and is in short a most humanitarian measure.

October 30, 1970
Emergency Cold Mining Assistance Act
Additional grants would not be a burden to the Canadian economy unduly because they would come back for the most part, if not completely, to the federal treasury in the form of income taxes, or direct or indirect taxes. Thus by helping industries of prime importance to survive, the prosperity of many areas would be ensured, which would allow to maintain the production of gold.
It is therefore very important that immediate action be taken, if we want not only our cities to survive, but to prosper and expand.
If we want northwestern Quebec to survive, a promising area with an almost unlimited potential but to which governments have not given enough importance, it is necessary to act immediately. Indeed, the population of that area, in 1959, was 51,800, and in 1969, it was 56,000. The gold mines employed 2,360 people in 1959 but only 1,930 in 1969. Their dependants, in 1959, totalled 5,900 and, in 1969, 5,000.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks which I wanted to make in connection with gold mines. On behalf of those citizens of northwestern Quebec, and of those of northeastern Ontario, who are in the same situation, I say again that the government can export to the United States the entire gold production of Canada. Indeed, we have a very important trade with that country. And I maintain that the government would then have at least the certainty of keeping its balance of payments with the United States within more reasonable limits than if it put an end to gold production.
On behalf of northwestern Quebec, in the name of the miners and especially of their families, I ask the government to be more generous. I am not begging but I ask the government to give assistance to the development of new gold mines in our region by encouraging prospection and getting the companies to invest there to save from stagnation an important proportion of our population and give our citizens the right to live in their country, Canada, and mainly in this part of the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), I am pleased to ask the House to approve second reading of this bill. I am sure members in all parts of the House appreciate that the heavy water plant at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, was planned a number of years ago and was to start production in 1966. It failed to do so because of faults in design. A massive investment by the province of Nova Scotia has been rusting away.
Consequently, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 10 of this year announced that the Government of Canada would provide to the government of Nova Scotia the substantial assistance necessary to rehabilitate the plant and get it into production.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The bill now before us will provide part of that assistance. At the time when the project was started, the area development agency approved the company's application for assistance to the maximum of $5 million under the legislation then operative. Under that legislation, the grant would have been paid only when the plant was in production. Moreover, the legislation under which ADA operated sets a termination date. To receive an ADA grant, a plant must be in production by March 31 next year, that is to say, some five months hence. This will not be possible in the case of Deuterium of Canada Limited. Parliament has given the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) authority to grant time extensions, but only when the reasons for delay are beyond the control of the people establishing the plant.
In the Deuterium case, the failure to meet the deadline is due not to external factors but to technical difficulties which clearly must be regarded as the responsibility of the people putting up the plant. Accordingly, the Area Development Incentives Act cannot be used to make the intended $5 million grant.
All members will agree that this has been a difficult and financially burdensome problem for the government of Nova Scotia. That government believes the plant can be rehabilitated, but substantial further expenditures are required. Opposition spokesmen, as recorded in Hansard for April 10 last, welcomed the Prime Minister's announcement of the federal government's intention to help the government of Nova Scotia with these expenditures. We, in this House, all recognize that it would be tragic if the large capital investments already made had to be abandoned. One way to save the government of
[Mr. Caouette.l
October 30, 1970

Nova Scotia from that situation is to pay the $5 million which was expected when the project was launched with the aim of being in production long before the legislative deadline for ADA grants.
Since special legislation would now be required to make this payment, we propose to take the opportunity to ease Nova Scotia's financial problems to a further extent by asking Parliament, through this bill, to authorize payment of the grant in instalments as the rehabilitation of the plant proceeds. This is more advantageous than the normal ADA provision for paying the grant only after production has started.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the substance of this piece of legislation. I believe hon. members on both sides of the House regard it as a necessary contribution to the economy of Cape Breton. On behalf of the minister I, therefore, ask approval of the bill to authorize a grant to the province of Nova Scotia for the purpose of assisting Deuterium of Canada Limited.

The arrangements that have been made concerning the advancement of moneys by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited will certainly be helpful in respect of the first year's production.
I think the question that has been uppermost in the minds of most people for some time concerned the availability of the new management, now under the
Deuterium of Canada Assistance Bill direction of Mr. R. B. Cameron and Mr. Nazzer, who is considered to be one of the outstanding authorities in this field. Under their direction the rehabilitation of this plant should be successful. We are grateful that this bill has been brought forward at this time so that the rehabilitation will get underway as quickly as possible. Despite statements to the contrary, the Nova Scotia government of Mr. G. I. Smith worked long and faithfully on this case, and under the direction of Mr. Cameron and Mr. Nazzer I believe the situation has been brought to a point where this financial assistance will get this plant off the ground. Under the management of these two very capable persons the rehabilitation will take place. This, of course, will be a great source of aid and comfort to the people of Cape Breton and, as I said, Nova Scotia as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of us have long been concerned about the development of this heavy water plant in Nova Scotia, particularly because, despite the planning done many years ago to ensure that we would have a plant that would produce heavy water, as yet none of that commodity has been produced. Many of us are aware of the difficulties the Maritime Provinces are having. We are aware also of the fact that much of their hope for additional development in that area stems from the production of this plant which would have a number of by-products. Hopefully, this should be the basis for the creation of a totally new industry in this province which would make it much more self-sufficient.
Some of us will be reluctant to pass this bill at this time. I say that because of the events that have taken place in the past few months, particularly the statements made by one of the cabinet ministers in that area who said, in effect, to the Conservative government that until it brought forward new plans that would indicate some hope of success in the development of this plant, the $41 million the federal government had tentatively agreed to provide would not be provided. It is very interesting to note that that cabinet minister now seems to have no objection to the paying of this $5 million grant to the province, partly because of the change in government. I certainly give the government credit when I say that that is not the reason for proceeding with this bill. This bill was prepared originally some time ago. I have checked it and find it to be identical with the bill that was before us much earlier. In fact, it was first dated June 15, 1970, so this bill is not new and it was not brought in because of the change in government.

Mr. Speaker, the assistance provided by the federal government to the government of Nova Scotia under this bill was negotiated by the previous provincial government of the Hon. G. I. Smith, and was announced in this House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 10 last. At that time I had an opportunity to make a few remarks on the general problem, and now I am pleased to note that the new Nova Scotia government has confirmed the correctness of the previous decision to proceed to bring the plant into production of heavy water.
There is no doubt about the fact that power sources in Canada are gradually diminishing. They are certainly falling behind projected requirements. New sources of water power are becoming scarcer. The use of coal in the production of power is also diminishing to a considerable extent, and so we must turn to nuclear energy to provide electric power for Canada's future needs. To keep our nuclear power plants operating, it is necessary that heavy water be produced in Canada. The decision to proceed with the establishment of heavy water nuclear plants in Canada was made many years ago because it seemed that Canada had the best source of uranium, and to that time had done the most extensive work undertaken in connection with the peaceful use of atomic power.
I was a member of a special committee of this House, I believe it was in 1960, which examined research in Canada, when the government's decision was discussed by a great many eminent scientists. At the end of very extensive hearings, the decision was confirmed that Canada should continue to develop heavy water nuclear power plants. In the light of this history, the only possibility left is to proceed with this plant at Glace Bay, providing the engineering is successful. I presume that the engineering problems have now been mastered, or that at least the engineers see the possibility of being successful in bringing the plant into production. The
Deuterium of Canada Assistance Bill sooner that happens the better it will be not only for the people of Cape Breton-East Richmond but also for the whole of Canada.

Heavy water is a product that can be made commercially. There is no radiation, nor atomic aspects connected with it. It is only confusing to compare it with the role that Atomic Energy of Canada might play in advising on the design of atomic reactors, as was the case in Ontario.
This is not an atomic reactor; it is a heavy water plant. Canadian General Electric is producing it as a product, like any other product. It is just water that is 10 per cent heavier than usual. It had to enter into a contract for that, but the responsibility for production of heavy water was the responsibility of the private company that began the operation, and it became the responsibility of the province when it assumed that responsibility from the private company.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
This very interesting motion, Mr. Speaker, gives members of the House an opportunity to deal with several aspects of a matter to which reference has already been made. The motion reads:
That the Public Accounts for the year ended March 31, 1969, and the Auditor General's Report thereon, and the evidence adduced by the Committee during the past Session in relation thereto be referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.
Of course you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of the House, will notice that this motion is included on the Order Paper as a government order. This is the result of a policy which has been announced by this party and, hopefully, supported by my friends who sit on my left, to this effect: that, with regard to the appointment, the operations and the terms of reference of committees generally, we are not prepared to be as free and easy as we have been in the past. This matter was discussed and the issues were referred to in the debate this House embarked upon at the time of the establishment of the joint committee of this House and the other place to deal with the constitution.
At that time, on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, I made certain points. I did so in a very friendly way and I propose to be reasonably friendly today. The points I made then were these: that we were becoming very concerned about the operation of committees and about the impact they were having on the capacity of this House to function efficiently and properly as a forum wherein could be debated the affairs of the people of Canada. It was because of our experience with committees last year, not only of this House but of the other

October 30, 1970
place-we have a vested interest in the operations of committees in the other place because we are both part of the Parliament of Canada-that we made it quite plain that from that time on, all motions dealing with committees would have to be placed on the order paper; that unanimous consent would not be given; and that it would be essential that there be at least an opportunity for discussion. Pursuant to that policy, the government placed on the order paper the terms of reference for the appointment of a number of committees, including this one.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
A short time ago the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) placed on record his consent on behalf of this party to the establishment of some of these committees, but consent was deliberately withheld with respect to this committee so that it would provide a vehicle for discussion and an opportunity to renew the interesting debate we had earlier on this subject.
I might say in passing that there are a number of areas of concern to us. One is the question of cost. We are concerned about the cost because the people of Canada are much concerned about the level of taxation. They want to know what Parliament is doing, what its operations are costing and whether all of them are necessary. It is with this in mind that I called into question the extent to which the joint committee on the constitution was proposing to become involved in a travelling program of a substantial nature in accordance with the power sought, and granted, of journeying from place to place.
I should note in passing that the report filed by the co-chairman of the committee this morning makes provision for travelling all over Canada during a period of 45 days from the time the session began until the end of June. The cost involved here might well be substantial. However, I shall go no further on these lines, because I would not be allowed to do so. I draw attention to this matter, however, because we entered a caveat at the time we first held our discussion on this subject. We made our views known at that time, but no notice has been taken of them. Since then, some interesting information has come to us from the other place, information which emphasizes the desirability of providing means whereby this House would have some degree of control after committees have been appointed on motions of this kind. These things should not be left to the committees themselves or to the good offices of Mr. Speaker, who is sometimes left in a difficult position.
The evidence indicates that well over one million dollars has been disbursed so far with respect to two committees of the other place, and more will yet be spent. As was demonstrated by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales), who spoke in the last debate on this subject, the possible costs of the committee to which 1 have been referring will be an amount of similar magnitude. For this reason, whenever there is a motion before us to set up a committee, we intend to bring our concern about these matters to the attention of the House. When a
Public Accounts
million dollars is being spent, I want to know, and my hon. friends want to know, that good value will be obtained for it in the circumstances which prevail today.
Another area of our concern is the extent to which the multiplicity of our committees is reducing the operations of this House to a nullity. I know there are problems. I know we are learning as we go along. The other day I was reading a report brought in by the new leader of the house in the United Kingdom, Mr. Whitelaw. Some members of this House, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) had an opportunity on one or two occasions both here and elsewhere to meet members of the United Kingdom Parliament and discuss our experience with them. Members of the British Parliament were very interested in our committee system, but they warned us: do not go too far or too fast or you will remove all the emphasis from the House and place it on the committees, and the chamber of the House of Commons will cease to be what it has been for so long, the central pivot of our democratic system.
1 notice that at Westminster they have gone moderately along the path we have taken by setting up specialized committees to deal with some of their work. I intend, later in my remarks, to commend in the highest terms the Public Accounts Committee. It has carried out its function in an admirable and non-partisan way, and what I have said so far does not apply to that body. But I am using this motion as a peg upon which to hang words of warning to the House, and to the government, with respect to possible abuse of the committee system. When I see only a score or so of members in this chamber, as happens every day of the week, I know there are large numbers of our members who are engaged in committee work or engaged on their constituency duties. But 1 believe it is incumbent upon us to pattern the committee structure on the basis that this House is the central point around which all the activities of Parliament should revolve.
We ought to examine every proposal to set up a committee in the fight of this responsibility, and I can assure hon. members that I intend to do this from time to time in the hope that the government will take up the suggestion I made at the time of the last debate on this subject, a suggestion which was echoed by other opposition members. The time has come, in the fight of our experience during the past one and a half years, for the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to review the operations of House committees so as to ensure that the difficulties and the faults which have been so obvious, and to which attention has been drawn time and time again by my hon. friends on this side of the House, are removed and that necessary reforms are introduced. If this is not done, the committee structure will collapse and bring down with it much of the value of debate in this House.
The Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Jerome) was a valuable member of the special committee which was the forerunner of the present standing committee, so I am sure he would be the first to acknowledge that the system

October 30, 1970
Public Accounts
which we introduced was experimental in nature. The stage has now been reached at which many of the reforms we brought in then need to be modified in the light of our experience. I am not suggesting that the committee should meet tomorrow and bring forth changes the following day. I recognize that the committee has other responsibilities. But there is no reason why a sub-committee should not be set up to deal with this matter. One has only to hear the outpourings of dissatisfaction and annoyance coming from private members, particularly those on this side of the House, to realize that something ought to be done by way of improvement. But this warning is by way of a preliminary to what I have to say about the particular committee we are being asked to consider this afternoon.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I am glad to see that the public accounts committee is going to be re-established. This is one committee in which, certainly over the last 12 years-with one exception last year with which I propose to deal later-there has been a sort of non-partisan, objective approach on the part of a number of Members of Parliament operating on behalf not only of their constituents but of all the people of Canada. They have examined, scrutinized and challenged the cost of government under capable leadership and brought to the attention of the people of Canada details of extravagances, aided by the Auditor General and the officials of departments who have appeared before them.
Ever since 1958 when the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), as Prime Minister of the day, re-established the committee as a viable and useful entity with a member of the opposition to chair it-now a member of the other place-the committee has had a very effective and useful life and has done yeoman service for the people of Canada.
For that reason, I am glad to see the committee being set up under terms of reference embracing the report of the Auditor General. I think we are lucky to have a very valuable and useful occupant of that position today. It is interesting to note that there have been, I do not know how many Prime Ministers, 15 or 16-there may be some scholars on the other side who can tell me the exact number we have had-yet there have been only six Auditors General.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: The number is 15.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I thought at times the number might have been 13, but I am now told it is 15. However, there have been only six Auditors General in the same period. The present occupant brings a lot of useful character and knowledge to the position. It is of interest to note that during the last few days he was unanimously recommended for re-appointment as Auditor General of the United Nations, this being his third term. I think this inures to the benefit of Canada and it is of some satisfaction to us to realize the value of the present Auditor General. However, I would not be fulfilling my duty in
speaking to the House today if I failed to point out that by an anomaly, as far as salary is concerned, which is one of the matters dealt with in the evidence that the motion asks to be referred back to the committee, the Auditor General receives substantially less than his assistant.
In the area of the accountability of governments for spending, I think this is a shocking condition. I hope that when the committee is appointed under its terms of reference, as I am sure it will be, the committee will turn its attention to this particular problem. Some recommendations were made by the committee. I agree with some, I disagree with others, and I must say that there were some that could only be compared with the perverse verdict of a jury in the face of overwhelming evidence before them. However, as I say, one of the matters that must be dealt with by this committee is this salary situation. The qualifications of the assistant Auditor General are very high, and I have great respect for him personally. Yet under the terms of the statute that now governs the operations of the Auditor General and his office, we find this very ridiculous situation prevailing. When the committee is established, I hope it will see fit to turn its attention to this particular issue.
The need today for this committee in terms of the examination made by the Auditor General is very high. This is an age of bureaucrats, and we have a government of bureaucrats. I am not against bureaucrats; indeed, we have to have them today, though we have a particularly invidious group sitting opposite us who are well schooled in the art of being a bureaucrat. However, it is helpful to know that in order to meet the challenge of bureaucracy it is essential to have a public accounts committee, and that it is essential to have terms of reference that permit the closest and most detailed examination of the operations of the bureaucracy as it is spread throughout each department. This, in turn, involves some examination of the changes made in the functions of the Auditor General. This is one reason that the terms of reference to which I have referred included the requirement, as an integral part of the motion, that the evidence taken before the committee last session should be referred to the present committee.
On this issue, as well as on the issue of the relationship of the committee to the Auditor General and of the Auditor General to the government, it is fascinating to read in the evidence, evidence that is quite relevant in this context, some of the statements that were made by Professor Norman Ward, probably the outstanding and acknowledged authority on the public purse, the operations of the Auditor General and the public accounts committee. His credentials are impeccable. He is objective and non-partisan. He is the author of several books and was apparently the last witness to appear before the committee last session. I should like to put on the record before I conclude some of his evidence in the hope that what Professor Ward said will commend itself to members of this committee. When they come to deal with this particular aspect of the functions and duty of the Auditor General, and to deliberate thereupon, I hope they will not

October 30, 1970

fail to remember what Professor Ward said and to bear it well in mind.
I was speaking about bureaucrats a few moments ago. There is no doubt that there was on the part of government members opposite, and certainly on the part of every member of the administration, a quite obvious and demonstrated attempt to cut down the functions of the Auditor General. The Auditor General had annoyed them: they did not like his criticism. If I ever found an Auditor General who said things that appealed to the government, then I would say he ought to be fired on the spot. No government, particularly one of this size, can fail to make errors of judgment, to over-spend, to be guilty of being improvident, to engage in non-productive payments. That is part of the game and we must expect it. This is why we must have committees, and officials like the Auditor General, who function on behalf of the taxpayer, who will be breathing down the necks of departments, bureaucrats and deputy ministers and saying to them: "Hold on a minute, you are going the wrong way. What are you doing here?" Report must then be made to the House in elaboration of their findings.
When we see, as we saw last year, the then President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), who has now gone forward into a higher echelon of bureaucracy, and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) making statements that constitute an obvious attempt to relegate the Auditor General to the performance of functions that were subservient to those he had exercised before, it must serve as a warning to all of us, particularly to members of the opposition. This will not be tolerated.
Let me put on the record at this stage the statement that if this government attempts to bring in new legisla-ion of a kind envisaged by the former President of the Privy Council and eagerly supported by some of his colleagues, this legislation is going to run into the toughest kind of opposition there is from members on this side of the House. I give that warning to the government right now. Having said that, I leave my few remarks in, I hope, a spirit of amity and friendliness. I hope the hon. members who serve on the committee will take these remarks very much to heart.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
I have before me the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on public accounts, number 33 dated June 16, 1970. These proceedings took place just before the committee brought down its recommendations to the House. This is part of the evidence that is now being sought to be placed before the new committee. Let me read some of the things Professor Ward said. I should love to put it all on the record, but it will be on the record of the committee.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is quite a lengthy report and I wonder if the page number could be given just to assist the members?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Yes, I had intended to give the page number, Mr. Speaker. I hope the hon. member will take
Public Accounts
this report home, read it and cogitate on it over the weekend. I read from page 33:6 from Professor Ward's evidence:
I am aware, and I think it is to the eternal credit of the present government, that for the first time in Canadian history the opposition parties have been given small sums of money-
I emphasize that word "small". He continues:
-for research purposes as parties. I have not yet been able to find out, particularly because I have not had time, how they are using the money and what for, hut I hope to. This is, I think, an enormously important step in the right direction, but when you consider that the total amount of money made available to the three opposition parties is around $225,000, as I remember, and the government on its side has behind it a civil service of over 300,000 people altogether, counting the Crown corporations, spending a budget which is now running into the dozens of billions of dollars, $225,000 or so for the opposition does not even qualify as a drop in the bucket as ammunition with which to prepare cases to criticize the government.
Those are Professor Ward's views, not necessarily mine, but I think the comment he makes is interesting. On the next page, 33:7, which is the seventh page of the 33rd volume, the professor is reported as follows:
I am disallowing here any kind of partisan interest-
I could use those words myself of Professor Ward; I am not disallowing any kind of partisan interest. He continues:
-from the point of view of a particular party, but it is a fact of life in Canada that for the past half century for all but 12 years, Canada has been governed by a party which never bestows its leadership on a seasoned parliamentary veteran. Without exception every single leader of the Liberals since Sir Wilfrid Laurier have been chosen in convention. Every one of them has beaten far more experienced parliamentarians for the leadership. This, I think, is probably one of the secrets of the party's success, perhaps-
That word "perhaps" is the professor's word. To quote again:
-but it has as far as Parliament is concerned the rather curious by-product that for prolonged periods the Prime Minister of Canada is not himself a man experienced in sitting on committees such as this. I have not had time to check out all the committees in existence during all the years of the four people I have mentioned: Mr. King, Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Pearson, and now Mr. Trudeau. To the best of my recollection I have never encountered any of their names in the proceedings of a Parliamentary committee. They have had no experience.
I could add that there are one or two of them that have not had too much experience in Parliament either, Mr. Speaker, and certainly their records since they have become leaders show it. The professor goes on to say and I quote from the same page:
This again enormously enhances the importance of this Committee and the Auditor General who is Parliament's servant or particularly working with this committee. This is I think a uniquely Canadian phenomenon. I do not know of any other free country in which the leadership of a major party is in power most of the time is given not occasionally or even regularly, but all the time to somebody in effect who opted from outside. That, I think, is again one of the fundamental considerations that has to underline any consideration of the role of Auditor General in Canada, that he occupies a most

October 30. 1970
Public Accounts
peculiar position through no fault of his or anybody else's. The facts of Canadian party life just have worked out that way now for half a century.
I do hope the committee that is appointed for this year will give more serious consideration to those statements. There are so very few really effective and potent weapons available to an opposition party under the kind of system and statutes we have, which permit the government the right to operate in so many cases by Order in Council. To meet the vast forces of government and its supporting bureaucracy, we must have an official like the Auditor General working with a reinforced committee such as the Public Accounts committee.
Finally I have two more quotations from page 9 of the same issue. The first one reads:
This raises the question-which I presume will come up again later but I want to make sure that I put it on the record now because I wish to say something about it-whether or not the Auditor General should simply coniine himself to commenting on the legality or otherwise of expenditures or whether he should get himself involved in commenting on what is in effect policy from the point of view of the government.
I pause here because this is the crux of the argument which has developed between the cabinet on the one side and the Auditor General on the other. I am convinced that the two ministers whose names I used, or whose positions are used, did not speak out as they did in criticism of the Auditor General and his role without having behind them the full support of the government and the Prime Minister.
I think the words of Professor Ward must be engraved on the hearts of the members of the committee when they come to examine this problem. What are the functions of the Auditor General? Must he be confined within strict terms, as has been suggested by ministers on the other side, or should he have a degree of freedom which permits him an opportunity to go into other matters, which I submit is so essential? Let me continue with what Professor Ward said:
My general position on this, which I really have held for many years, is that there is no conceivable way in which you could limit an Auditor General to commenting only on the legality of expenditures-none. The reason I say that is that it is his duty, clearly, to report what he considers are extravagant or improvident expenditures.
I pause here to say what a great field he has when he serves with the gentlemen who sit opposite us. Then, to continue:
But they could be perfectly legal. I could be paid by the government $1,000 for $1,000 worth of work quite legally, but under the same kind of contract I could be paid $5,000 for doing $1,000 worth of work and it would be perfectly legal-and I think, it would be the duty of the Auditor General to point out that I had in fact been paid five times as much as the job is worth.
Just as simple as that in those clearly expressed terms, Professor Ward has pointed out the nub of the problem regarding the conflict between the government and the Auditor General. When we see the committee bring in recommendations, as they obviously attempted to do, which would take the government side, then I think

probably-I will not say there was a hatchet job because I think I would not be right in saying that-it is time to take stock. There were a few times when the committee obviously attempted, through government members, to carry forward the views of the then President of the Privy Council and to incorporate them in the terms of the recommendations of the committee.
I would like to see the committee review this, too, and the other evidence which was given last June. By reviewing and changing some of those recommendations in light of the clear warning uttered by Professor Ward, they would show themselves to be honourable and distinguished Members of Parliament.
[DOT] (2:40 p.ra.)

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Delighted.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: I am a member of the Public Accounts Committee, and 1 gather the hon. member is referring to the recommendation in respect of a new Auditor General's act. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never been an obsequious member of this House. If members on our side of the House in my judgment are mistaken, I would have no hesitation in saying so. This is a policy I would recommend to members opposite. It would be much better if members on the other side would stand up and criticize the government, especially when there is so much to criticize.
The quotation continues:
I hasten to add that this never has happened. But it could happen perfectly legally and it would certainly, I think in a case like that, still be the duty of the Auditor General, whether it was legal or not, to comment on what seemed to him to be an improvident expenditure.
I think this is extremely important, Mr. Speaker. I am just about finished. I hope I have excited other hon. members to get up and defend themselves and contribute to this very important debate which I believe is of great consequence to the people of this country who are saddled with a heavy burden of taxes which will become even greater if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has his way. Then, there is this paragraph on page 10:
I do not really know of any way either in which you can prevent the Auditor General from straying over, sometimes at least, even inadvertently, into the field of policy, because policy nowadays is not that clear-cut a thing that you can distinguish the purely financial aspect of policy from policy itself. One only has to consider for example how many of our major expenditures of government today-this again is very unlike the way things were in 1878-are substantive expenditures, like the family allowance, in which the actual administrative cost
October 30, 1970

is a tiny fraction of the total cost of the program. The Auditor General, if he confines himself solely to the purely legal administrative aspects of running this enormous program, in a case like this is simply going to have to neglect things that conceivably might be worth looking at because they are involved in some kind of policy. I will return to that point later.
Then, finally:
But my general view of this is that the Auditor General really cannot be narrowly confined to a purely legalistic view of his job if he is to do his job properly. Of course he is going to make mistakes-he is human, and of course he is going to aggravate the government-they are human.
I sometimes doubt that statement.
And he should make mistakes and aggravate the government rather than overlook things that ought to be drawn to the public's attention. It is far better that he should be free to make mistakes in the same way that the Supreme Court judge is free to make mistakes than that he should be hampered so that he is afraid to make mistakes.
With that, I shall leave my comments before the House. I say again that in the kind of world in which we live, and with the kind of governments we have in this country and in the United States where the Congressional elections will be held next Tuesday, one of the major issues is the very issue of government expenditures and taxes which are reflected in the cost of living. Any attempt to curtail or limit the powers and functions of the Auditor General or of the Public Accounts Committee would be a great mistake. I urge the committee when it commences its deliberations to bear these things in mind.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to use any further time of the House on this somewhat routine measure but, as we had anticipated, some of the things the House Leader of the Opposition has said certainly require some comment from this side of the House. I am only too happy to make those comments. 1 assume I am eligible to reply to the hon. member because, not having risen as high as the ministry and not being in the civil service, I am not subject to that very wide designation of his of being a bureaucrat, which seems to cover just about every one who has views opposite to his. In any event, I think the very subject of this motion, to refer certain matters to the Public Accounts Committee, leads us to a consideration of some of the fine work that was undertaken by this committee during the last session. I think it is significant that co-operation between the parties in this House has led to this vehicle being on the order paper.
We learned that the hon. member had some comments he wished to make in this connection and, accordingly, this matter was held over until this time in order to give him an opportunity to deliver the comments he has delivered today. We are prepared to have these matters discussed because the committee system is an extremely important part of the operations of this Parliament so far as the government is concerned. However, I think the references made by the hon. member to the Auditor General's Act are entirely unfair. I think anyone would
Public Accounts
agree that last year, regardless of what I think was a very unnecessary political attitude on the part of many members of the House-the most unfortunate atmosphere possible-the whole subject was considered. I think the hon. member will agree with me that, despite the political connotations, legitimate progress was made in respect of that very important statute. I see that the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales), who was chairman of the committee at that time is here, as is the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Bigg). I am sure they and other members who were members of the committee will agree with me that, notwithstanding the extremely difficult and strained atmosphere, the work of the committee progressed very well and that, in fact, there were great accomplishments.
Therefore, I take great issue with the hon. member's reference to this subject because it would seem to be a condemnation of the work of the committee. I take it as the very strongest commendation that even under such difficult conditions the committee made great progress and accomplished many things in much less time than would have been possible under the former rules of the House.
Before leaving this subject, I should like to refer to one other matter pertaining to the same Public Accounts Committee. I refer to the time when very considerable tariff concessions to the Ford Motor Company were debated by members opposite.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: You gave them $10 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) is again off the subject. This matter was extremely political, in view of the stand taken by members opposite, when it was discussed by the Public Accounts Committee. I am sure members opposite will agree that the kind of investigation that was carried out in the committee would not have been possible if the matter had been dealt with by the Committee of the Whole House. These tariff concessions were discussed with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and members of his staff, as well as senior representatives from the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance. If any question involving tariffs comes up in the course of the debate on estimates or in the course of the debate of a subject that is before the Committee of the Whole House, a minister has the opportunity from time to time to evade questions by saying that that area of questioning should fall to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) or else to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). That kind of escape is possible here in the House. But the kind of examination that took place in the Finance Committee would not permit that type of escape. The resulting detailed examination that was available through the Committee procedure gave all hon. members on both sides of the House, an unparalleled opportunity to examine that important question in detail. So, I think that the importance of the committee system is self evident. In addition, one should remember that last year some 1,200 hours were spent collectively by the standing committees on the examination of

October 30. 1970
Public Accounts
legislation, in fact about twice as much time as was spent by this chamber.
[DOT] {2:50 p.m.)
So, there is certainly a very clear case for the work that is being done in the standing committees and for the entire committee system. When hon. members opposite question the cost, I think it is fair to examine these things because it is not just the cost but the value received that has to be considered. When one sees the number of hours spent in detailed clause by clause examination of legislation and of departmental estimates, in the sort of detail that is possible in the committees but not possible here, one realizes the importance of the committee system. We are in conflict at all times on at least two counts: first, this House is a debating society in the true sense of the word and second, it is important that everyone has time to speak in this chamber on subjects of their choice.
At the same time, we already sit in this chamber as many hours in the day and days in the year as it is possible. The schedule to which we adhere at present cannot be stretched much more. This means that we are in conflict in so far as efficiency is concerned. This place cannot go on maintaining the respect of the citizenry if it does not do its business efficiently. We are using all the available time and we must keep up with the business. The result is that the committee system presents a golden opportunity to make the procedures of the House more efficient, because the matters that have to be discussed can be discussed in the House as well as in several standing committees at the same time. The item of the most fundamental importance is to ensure that through participation in the affairs of the standing committees the whole system is made to contribute and to complement the function of the House, not to compete with it. That, I think, is the problem.
In addition, we are in another conflict which I think is very important because we, who are directly involved in the affairs of this chamber, become knowledgeable about what happens here. We are all elected representatives; we are very much involved in politics and in government, and consequently we tend to think that everyone in the country knows and cares about these matters as much as we do. In fact, they do not. In fact, the great majority of our citizens not only do not know a great deal about the political life of the country or the function of their government, but they do not care.
It is an important function of Parliament as a whole to fulfil an educative role, to take the government, at least to some extent, to the people; to get out to the country and function in other centres than the very much confined space of these buildings. The committee system can do this. When a committee travels to Vancouver or to Halifax or to any of the smaller or more remote centres-and here I am addressing myself to hon. members from the areas outside the major metropolitan centres- the government is brought closer to the people. Hon. members know that they represent people who feel they are very much out of the main stream of events; they are
away from provincial capitals and from the national capital.
I think it is a very important duty and function of Parliament to attempt to bring the government to those people and, so far as possible, to let those people participate in and see government functioning in their own centres. The committees that travel about the country, as well as working at the time that they are there, fulfil that very important function. So, we have the conflict of efficiency as opposed to the debating society approach which enables everybody to hold up the work of this House and carry on until everyone has had a chance to speak. We also have the conflict of centralizing the government in Ottawa as opposed to bringing it to the people.
These are the conflicts that have to be borne in mind when hon. members say that the committee system is detracting from the business of the House and from the importance of this chamber. I will go along with the hon. member in attempting, as he was, to be non-partisan because I do not suggest for one minute that what I am about to say here does not tar us and hon. members opposite with the same brush. The plain truth is that in theory the committee system at present is not bad.
