subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The question probably refers to the member's suggestion to review the committee system by referring the matter to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. He said that in order to precipitate this course, if necessary, he is prepared to debate every routine motion for reference to a standing committee until he has made his point about expenses. We are quite prepared to examine, with a very careful eye, the proposed expenses of the committees.
I am speaking from personal experience as the immediate past chairman of the special committee on election expenses, which sat for a very short period in the last session. One of the first subjects that we discussed-and opposition members who were on that committee will support me on this-was whether that committee needed to travel. Because there is a system in the province of Nova Scotia that would have been of interest to the committee, because there is one in the province of Quebec, because there are different electoral systems in various provinces throughout the country and, in fact, in other countries throughout the world, there would have been every justification for the committee applying to the house for permission to travel. The subject was discussed and I think hon. members opposite will agree that, as chairman of the committee, I expressed the opinion as forcibly as I could that the right thing for the committee to do was to stay here, unless members felt there was some worthwhile work that could be done.
I am happy to say that members of all parties were agreed. I submit that as an example of the proper attitude taken by committee members of all parties with respect to the expenditure of money on committees.
[DOT] (3:00D.m.)
It is all very well for the hon. member opposite to suggest a review by the Procedure and Organization Committee, but it is only fair to put on record that at the end of last session the government was anxious that some arrangement be made whereby that committee could review all the rules of the House, and do it on a continuing basis. We still stand in support of that proposition. The hon. member opposite knows that his party has taken a position opposed to that. We have been anxious to give the committee not only the power, on an ad hoc basis if necessary, to review the rules governing committees but also, if it is preferred by the House, to give it a standing reference covering all the rules of the House. In our view this would be a sensible arrangement.
That suggestion has met with opposition from the other side of the House. Again I say we submit that the proper thing to do is to have the committee not only discuss the rules pertaining to committees but have it constantly discuss, and consequently recommend, changing and updating of all the rules of the House. Participation by members of this House is what will make the committee system function as it should. I repeat that we are perfectly prepared to have the committees' rules, along with all
Public Accounts
the rules of the House, placed under constant review by the Procedure and Organization Committee.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say concerning the motion to refer certain work to the Public Accounts Committee. Speaking as a past chairman of that committee, there are one or two observations I would like to make. I compliment the government for calling this motion at an early stage in the session, as a matter of fact on the seventeenth sitting day. I have seen sessions which have gone on for months before any work was referred to that committee. This raises another point. The Public Accounts Committee recommended to the House that its members should be appointed for the duration of a Parliament. That recommendation was acted upon and now members are appointed to the committee for a whole Parliament. Members appointed for a whole Parliament provide continuity of work and research.
We also suggested that the Auditor General's Report be automatically referred to the committee when tabled and that it should not be left to the whim of the government when to refer the report. As yet that recommendation has not been acted upon and the committee only functions at the whim of the government. As a matter of fact, if the government does not want the committee to examine the Auditor General's Report, it does not have to refer the report to it. This is one of the committee's recommendations that should be acted upon by this Parliament.
We should stop and take note of the very inadequate way in which the Public Accounts Committee must function. For that committee we have one clerk. That is the extent of our staff. This is no reflection on our clerk. We have been fortunate in the Public Accounts Committee in that we have had excellent clerks, but for example when we were investigating expenditures in connection with the Bonaventure, the shipping company which did the refit came before us with its whole staff and also legal counsel. We did not even have legal counsel although we were dealing with a very intricate problem.
In the United Kingdom the public accounts committee has a staff of 10 or 12 people. They do not work just while the House sits. That committee functions the year round and is equipped to do the job for which it is established. So far as our Parliament is concerned, we are only scratching the surface and I strongly urge that our Public Accounts Committee be given better facilities, better accommodation, better staff and be set up for a year-round operation.
Any government that has an expenditure of about $13 billion a year certainly warrants a good, strong Public Accounts Committee. I believe the Public Accounts Committee functions as well as or better than any other committee of the House simply because we have done our best to keep it non-partisan. Granted, at times this was difficult, but all members of the committee, regardless of party affiliation, realized they were dealing with the expenditure of taxpayers' money, be they Liberal taxpayers, Conservative taxpayers or others. Members of

October 30, 1970
Public Accounts
the committee had one objective-that the money be spent wisely and properly. After all, Mr. Speaker, what other control have we in this House except when the departmental estimates are before us? I am sorry to say that under present arrangements, when departmental estimates are referred to committees they are not getting the close supervision that they should be getting and the publicity that should accompany them.
Once this House passes the estimates, the various government departments are given authority to spend the money granted by the House, and we must depend upon experienced civil servants to spend that money wisely and justly. When they do not, it is the responsibility of the Public Accounts Committee to call the civil servants before it and inquire why the money was not spent in a productive way. We in the Public Accounts Committee must deal with non-productive items. "Non-productive" is a hard word to define, but the committee has asked the Auditor General to list what he considers non-productive expenditures.
The House Leader of our party has called attention to the very fine report that Professor Ward made to the committee, and I recommend that all hon. members read it. The Public Accounts Committee has functioned well for the past 13 years under its present system. I sincerely hope we will able to continue on that basis, in a non-partisan way, dealing with the issues that the Auditor General brings to our attention. If the Auditor General does not have a good Public Accounts Committee to answer to, we will have a poor Auditor General, because the two go together. The committee, as it were, is his right arm. If we are to have a strong, viable Auditor General we must have a strong, viable, energetic Public Accounts Committee.
When the proposed Auditor General of Canada act comes before us, Mr. Speaker, I shall have only one plea to make. I hope this House will not do anything to curtail the powers of the Auditor General. In business, if you call in an auditor to audit the books of a company you do not say to him, "I just want you to look at that and that" and tell him what you want him to do. You do not lay before him a list of things you want him to do. You say, 'There are the books. Audit them and bring to our attention anything that is not correct, any place where there has been non-productive spending, and show us what we can do to improve the operation of our business." So it should be with the business of the federal government.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I am sure that other hon. members wish to say some words on this subject. This has been a good opportunity for the House to comment on the operations of the Public Accounts Committee. I close by saying, as I did at the beginning, that I am pleased the government acted so quickly in calling the motion to refer this matter to the Public Accounts Committee.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate has ranged over a very wide area,

and I wish to make it clear that I do not intend to touch on all the aspects of the matter that have been discussed by those who have preceded me. As a matter of fact, I rise to deal with one particular point about which I feel rather strongly; but I admit that before I get to that main point there is one temptation that I really cannot resist. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), when talking about committees and how much they cost, referred to the fact that two of the committees of the other place had expenses during the last session, or at least over whatever period he was quoting, totalling $1 million. Four hundred and ninety-seven thousand dollars were spent on the Committee on Poverty. Some poverty! Also, $515,000 was spent on the Committee on Mass Media. If you add to that $442,000 for the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and $435,000 for the Committee on Science Policy, you are reaching a figure of almost $2 million.
Since suggestions are being made about steps that should be taken to save money, there is one obvious suggestion which I thought the hon. member for Peace River would make, namely, abolish the Senate. There is no use beating around the bush; let us deal with these things directly.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: The last NDP member who said that went to the Senate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: You should be with some of your own up there, Stanley.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS AND REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The hon. member is asking about some of my friends up there. All their lives they have been in favour of abolishing the Senate, and I trust they still are. After they have been there a while they will probably be even more in favour of doing so.
The main point I want to discuss is what I regard as the increasing importance that attaches to the work of the Public Accounts Committee. The thoughts which I have in mind I have already expressed in other ways and on previous occasions. Let me say that in my view we have not yet solved the problem of parliamentary control over government expenditures before they are made. We used to have the committee of supply. One hundred years ago Members of Parliament thought that through the committee of supply they did control the public purse, and perchance they were right. In recent decades that has not been true. As a matter of fact, we have more or less recognized that fact by abolishing the committee of supply and we now send all the estimates to various Standing Committees.
I think that most of the committees do a very good job and in some respects I think their work has been improved. However, it would be a wild and foolish Member of Parliament who would assert that the committees that examine estimates are scrutinizing public spending as the public feels it should be done. We just have not been doing the job and we have not solved the problem of how to do it. In fact, it is the one aspect of
October 30. 1970

the massive rules changes that we have made in the last two or three years which I think is still unfinished business.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want what I am going to say now to imply that we should let that go by the board. I think we should still find some way, in advance of the spending of money, for Parliament to check on it. But until we do find the way it becomes all the more important that we have this ex post facto check by the Public Accounts Committee. Sometimes it is argued that it is too late, that the money has been spent. The fact of the matter is that turning the searchlight on illegal or extravagant expenditures does have a salutary effect. I think that function must be stepped up, and I agree with the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) that the staff and assistance to the Public Accounts Committee ought to be increased.
There is something else we ought to consider, Mr. Speaker. Often we are told that the Auditor General does more than just give a report after the fiscal year is over, more than just lay it before us on the basis of what happened after the event is all over, but that he does a running audit right throughout the year. We are frequently told that he finds many things that need to be corrected and which are corrected right on the spot. It has also been suggested that sometimes he finds things that he thinks are wrong and has arguments with those in charge of the various departments. He may or may not win the arguments.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we might step up the process by which the Public Accounts Committee gets at these matters by making provision for the Auditor General to appear before the Public Accounts Committee on a current basis and to report to that committee some of the difficulties he is encountering. I adopt the language of the hon. member for Wellington when he said that the Public Accounts Committee is the Auditor General's right-hand man. I think it is true that you have a good Auditor General if you have a good Public Accounts Committee, and vice versa.
I strongly urge that we give some thought to this matter. Let us face the fact that what we used to do in committee of supply is not being done. Let us face the fact that the only effective check on expenditures before they are made is that which is made by the Treasury Board before we ever see the blue book of estimates. I am not satisfied with that, but such is the situation. That being the situation, I think that the kind of checking done by the Public Accounts Committee has to be stepped up. There has to be more of it, and there will have to be arrangements such as I have just suggested by which the Auditor General could report to the Public Accounts Committee on a current basis.
I am repeating myself, Mr. Speaker, but let me put it this way. Precisely because we do not have the kind of parliamentary control over the purse-strings that we think we have, or at least think we ought to have, the work of the Public Accounts Committee becomes all the more important. I am glad that we have this institution of an opposition member being appointed chairman of
Public Accounts
that committee. I certainly support those who express the view that the committee has been doing better work in the last decade than used to be the case. Let us strengthen it in every way we can, because it is pretty important in this massive expenditure operation that is modern government that there be a reasonable check on that expenditure by those of us who represent the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) wants to make a statement on Bill C-174, so I shall be brief in order that he will have time for his remarks. I wish to deal with two points. I listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Jerome), and I think he overlooked one thing. There is a difference between the functions of the members who sit behind the executive, the government, and the functions of those who sit in the opposition. We have to scrutinize matters in this chamber.
There are only 72 members in my party and we are always in attendance. The other parties can speak for themselves. I realize this is not a new problem. I realize that the government must keep its members busy and so it has allocated them to various committees. I am not a member merely of one committee. I am chairman of the justice caucus of our party and put a great deal of effort into that committee. I appreciate the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) saying that I attend committees. I do attend committees. But there are times when one has to be in the House. Hon. members must receive more co-operation. For instance, there are times when the Justice Committee is meeting and I have to be in the chamber on another matter.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
On one occasion, I believe it was on the expropriation bill, I asked that the matter be allowed to stand because I was presenting to this House during private members' hour a bill to amend the Criminal Code in connection with persons aged seven or older who might have committed a crime under the Code. I read in the newspaper that although I had been very active in the Justice Committee that afternoon, I was not present when the vote was taken with reference to the particular proposal I had opposed so strenuously. What I am saying is that you cannot be in two places at once.
I do not want to dig back into old history, but I remember Mr. Pickersgill, Mr. Pearson and Mr. Chevrier. When we had 208 members, forming a powerful government, they would not under any circumstances allow a committee to sit while the House was sitting. They realized, and I appreciated their position, that their job was to scrutinize the government's actions very carefully, to attempt, as we did yesterday, to secure amendments to certain legislation. It is very easy for the executive to present the bills. The executive sends its members to the committee.
Here is another thing I do not like about committees. I hear committees chairmen-this was particularly true of the Finance Committee-saying, "You are each going to have three minutes to speak." Isn't that a wonderful thought? If you were defending an accused in a courtroom and the judge said you had three minutes to cross-examine a witness you might barely get started on
October 30, 1970

it. It was a wonderful statesman's speech by the hon. member. These fellows grow to be statesmen. The more power they get, the more statesmanlike they become. This is the symptom of some appointment, some recognition.
We have to deal with this problem. The practical function that I have noticed-I do not mean the idealistic or the academic approach-of government members, basically, is that the chairman will say, "Here is a bill, and we are going to put it through in its present form." The minister hands out a little amendment to make it look as though we are intelligent. We think we are making amendments and changes and say, "This is a wonderful thing; this committee business is so refreshing." Well, gentlemen, let us not fool ourselves. When I am in a committee I do not want the chairman to say to me, while I am dealing with the question of capital gains-as we were in the Finance Committee-that I have two minutes. A number of people who have not done any studying whatsoever also have two minutes, and they are sweeping everything under the carpet while I am trying to get the facts on top of the table.
My job is not to praise the government: I leave that to others; there are enough backbenchers to do that. They all do it very well. My job and my function as long as I sit here-I hope to move over to the government side one of these days, and when hon. members over there now have my function I will listen to them-is to scrutinize very carefully, oppose if I think necessary, and suggest positive changes. So when I hear somebody get up and speak with those ideals, fold their arms and look to the sky and say that committees are non-partisan, I know that is tommyrot. The chairmen are picked; they are chosen by the men in power, the executive. They know when they go in there who is going to be chairman. I can name them before they are appointed. That is the way the committee system has been working.
There is merit to the new rules in some ways. There is merit attached to the committees in the United States. There is some merit attached to all systems and something to be learned from them all. I think the New Democratic Party should have some committee chairmanships. The Conservative party should have the chairmanship of some committees. The Creditistes should have some committee chairmanships. Then we will know that they are not partisan.
When we talk about all the amendments that are accepted, I know what these amendments turn out to be, even in our committee which works pretty well because most of us belong to the same profession. When you get a group of people from the same profession they have a sort of affection for each other aside from their political affiliations; we do work pretty well together. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if I had my way in this party, totally, and if I ran into the kind of thing I am talking about day after day, I would boycott the committees.

speechtext:
that Bill C-174, to establish the tax review board and to make certain amendments to other facts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not have too much time this afternoon, but I am delighted to have the opportunity of introducing a bill that represents the first major overhaul of the legislation relating to the review of income tax
and estate tax assessments by an administrative tribunal since the Tax Appeal Board was created in 1946.
Persons who are dissatisfied with the tax that a minister of national revenue has assessed against them under the provisions of the Income Tax Act or the Estate Tax Act at present have the right of having the dispute heard either by the Tax Appeal Board or the Exchequer Court of Canada. Since its creation in 1946, the present board has fulfilled a valuable and needed function. Many taxpayers have availed themselves of the right to go before the board in the first instance rather than to exercise their option to appear before the Exchequer Court. Experience has now shown, I think, that changes should be made to improve and to render more efficient the services performed by the board.
The Royal Commission on Taxation, under the chairmanship of the late Kenneth Carter, had as one of its recommendations the creation of a tax court with an appeal to a panel of three judges of the Exchequer Court. It was contemplated that the present Tax Appeal Board would be absorbed into the tax court. Those members interested should refer to pages 165 and 166 of volume 5 of the Carter report. If that recommendation were not acceptable, and the Tax Appeal Board were retained the Carter report recommended as an alternative the removing from it of the close association that it has with the Department of National Revenue, bringing it within the reporting authority of the Department of Justice. Its members should have the title, distinction and tenure of judges. It should have sole, original jurisdiction in all tax appeals, and provision should be made for discovery and production of documents. Again, members interested should refer to pages 164 and 165 of volume 5 of the Carter report.
The government and the House of Commons, by giving third reading to the federal court bill last night have adopted the primary recommendation of the Carter report that there should be a tax court, which in this case will be the trial branch of the new federal court. There will also be an appeal on the record to an appellate court, which will be the Court of Appeal for Canada. In that sense we have fulfilled that recommendation of the Carter commission.
After careful scrutiny of the work that is now being performed by the Tax Appeal Board, the government came to the conclusion that it would not be in the public interest that the board should be absorbed into the new federal court. It is our view that no good grounds can be advanced which would justify stripping the taxpayer of the existing privilege of appealing assessments either to an administrative tribunal like the Tax Appeal Board, with easy access, a minimum of complicated procedure' and no power to award costs in the event that the appeal was not successful or, if the taxpayer so wished, to a court of law, the Exchequer Court or the new trial division of the federal court.
There are many cases-I think hon. members will subscribe to what I say-where what is needed is an impartial tribunal which will, in an expeditious and inexpen-

October 30, 1970

sive manner, hear and adjudicate complaints which citizens, particularly citizens of modest means, have in respect of challenging assessments made against them. In such cases, a court of law, with its formal procedure for the discovery of documents, for settlement and adjudication of issues of fact and law, would unduly hamper and hinder the individual of modest means in obtaining a judgment at low cost, an impartial review with a minimum of procedural difficulty.
In this day and age of increasing bigness, remoteness and impersonality of government, it behooves the House of Commons, I believe, to take steps to see that not only is justice done but that to the public it appears to be done. One of the most significant changes introduced by the legislation now before the House which reconstitutes the Tax Appeal Board as a tax review board is that in future all persons who are appointed as members will hold office, as do judges, during good behaviour until they attain the age of 70 years. Under the existing legislation, members of the Tax Appeal Board can be appointed for a term of 10 years only. As pointed out in the Carter commission report, insecurity of tenure was one of the obstacles to the recruitment of members for the board.
Moreover, the appointment of members to hold office until 70 years of age will, in effect, provide the board with a greater degree of independence than in the present case where members hold office for ten years only, subject to reappointment. I submit that the bill will strengthen the independence of the tribunal because it will come under the general responsibility of the Minister of Justice and will not report to the Minister of National Revenue, as has heretofore been the case. These provisions reflect the recommendations made by the Carter commission.
In other words, having a board composed of members appointed for a limited term and reporting to the Minister of National Revenue, who happens to be one of the two parties to every suit, has given some people the idea that the board is not as impartial as it should be. I am not saying that the judgments handed down have not been reasonable judgments arrived at by reasonable human beings trying to do their best. But when members are subject to reappointment by the Minister of National Revenue and have a limited term of office, and one of the parties before the board is the person who represents the people of Canada and who appoints or may reappoint the member, I think there is the feeling that the board does not enjoy the independence it should enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, the new legislation specifies that the chairman and the assistant chairman must be members of a provincial bar or judges and that one or the other must have practiced law in the province of Quebec or must have been a judge of the Superior Court of Quebec. This last provision is meant to ensure at all times the presence of a chairman or of an assistant chairman who is fully conversant with the Civil Code of the Province of Quebec. This is a major aspect of the legislation, particularly when dealing with appeals about succession duties
Tax Review Board Bill
where the case at issue depends on the understanding of the rights and obligations prescribed in a will or other document whose interpretation is governed by a relevant provincial statute.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

One of the major purposes of the bill is to provide the ordinary taxpayer with a tribunal that combines accessibility, informality and effectiveness. In other words, it must be what it was originally meant to be in 1946, a taxpayer's court. The bill also provides that no special form of petition or pleading will be necessary to institute a review or an appeal from an assessment, and that the board is not to be bound by any legal or technical rules of evidence. The board is directed by the legislation to see that all appeals are dealt with as informally and expeditiously as the circumstances and considerations of fairness will permit.
Over the past few years-and the board has been in existence for almost 25 years-there necessarily has been built up a series of precedents, procedures and rules that have tended to make the board more formal and a little more cumbersome than it was originally intended to be. What I would like to do is strip it down again to what it was originally meant to be, namely, an informal board operating in an informal atmosphere where the taxpayer is able to come in-he does not need a lawyer, he can come in with a neighbour or a chartered accountant, representing himself or having anybody's help-to explain his case to the board in an informal way.
In the past, criticism has been made that if a taxpayer won before the Tax Appeal Board, the Minister of National Revenue, if the case involved a matter of interpretation so far as the law was concerned, or an important case that might create a precedent affecting numerous taxpayers, would appeal to the Exchequer Court. In the event the minister were successful in the appeal to the Exchequer Court, the taxpayer would normally be obliged to pay the costs that were awarded against him before the Exchequer Court.
I have felt for a long time that this created an unnecessary hardship on Canadian taxpayers and discouraged many people from taking an appeal before the appeal board. As a matter of fact, I can say there have been times when I was in private practice that I suspected the Department of National Revenue-and I think they will deny this-used the Tax Appeal Board as a method for hearing the taxpayer's case on discovery, that is to say, getting the basis of the taxpayer's case, and if they lost they would go to appeal and would have all the evidence they needed on which to build up their own case. I am not sure I could document this, but I have that suspicion.
I want to ensure that the Tax Appeal Board, or the new tax review board, cannot be used just as a preliminary step for the Department of National Revenue as a way of getting the taxpayer's case on the record. The proposed tax review board bill now before the House

October 30, 1970
Tax Review Board Bill
contains a provision for the modification of the Income Tax Act to provide that in any case where the Minister of National Revenue appeals a decision of the board to the court, and the amount of tax involved in the controversy does not exceed $1,000, the court is required, in delivering its judgment, to provide that the minister is to pay all reasonable and proper costs of the taxpayer in connection with the appeal to the court whether the taxpayer wins or loses. In other words, a taxpayer on an appeal in a matter involving less than $1,000 of tax assessed would have his appeal at the expense of the Crown, if he won in the first place.
Those are the broad areas of concern represented in the bill. I think it has to be read in conjunction with the federal court bill which passed this House last night on third reading, thanks to the courtesy of my friends on the opposite side. If the other place so provides, we will have a new federal court which will also be a court of first instance on tax matters. The taxpayer will have, and will continue to have under this bill, an alternative way of appealing tax assessments against him; an alternative way that will be less cumbersome than a court, less expensive and more informal and he will not need a lawyer.
We believe the taxpayer will be encouraged by the informal atmosphere and the opportunity to lay his case before an impartial tribunal rather than a group of men who are appointed for limited terms, appointed by the minister who happens to be one of the parties to the action. This board would be made up of men or women who may be lawyers, chartered accountants or from other disciplines. The president and the vice-president have to be lawyers, but the others need not. A taxpayer will have the chance to put his case before the board and he will have the right, of course, if he loses, to appeal to the federal court. On the other hand, if the minister appeals the case and the action involves less than $1,000, the taxpayer will not be penalized for having exercised this informal option.
I thank the House for this courtesy, and I thank particularly hon. members opposite who may have wanted to talk at great length on the matter that preceded this item. I am very grateful that I was given the opportunity of introducing the government's case on this bill.

I shall speak only on the procedural aspect, Mr. Speaker. I am a little surprised that this question is raised at this time, because if anything has been said in latter days regarding private members' bills, or public bills as they are called, certainly one criticism levelled at me was not that it was not procedurally correct.
So far as any charge to the treasury is concerned, of course that is completely out of the question, as is obvious in the bill. It says in very plain terms: "One of the members other than the president may be a Member of Parliament". It does not purport to add another member to the board, and in that case add any expense to the treasury in the event he would have to be displaced from one place to the other and have his expenses paid. Therefore, that Member of Parliament would simply be replacing any other member who may be appointed to the board of directors. So as far as the procedural aspect is concerned, frankly I am at a loss to understand why this question should have been raised.

Mr. Speaker, having looked at this bill, it seems to me that there are two possible points that can be raised in regard to it. The first is whether an additional charge is placed on the treasury by the terms of the bill. I have heard the explanation of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), who argues that the bill merely seeks to say that within the terms in which any Crown corporation would name its board of directors, one of them would be a Member of Parliament. There would be no increase in the total remuneration paid by that corporation and there would be no additional charge on public funds. In that respect it seems to me that this bill is beyond question within the terms of private members' bills which are permitted to be considered by the House.
The second question which should be raised is the possible conflict between the Senate and House of Commons Act. As members of the House are perfectly aware, that act prohibits members of the House from accepting remuneration in right of the Crown in any other employment or in other terms. These are broad and sweeping terms indeed. The question that has to be decided by hon. members is whether the terms of the bill as it is drafted would in fact resolve any possible conflict with the other piece of legislation.

It seems to me that the hon. member has attempted to anticipate this difficulty by stating in the clause "he shall be eligible for remuneration and expenses and shall not, by reason of his being the holder of the office or place in respect of which such remuneration and expenses are payable, be rendered incapable of being elected, or of sitting or voting, as a member of the House of Commons". These are the penalties prescribed by the Senate and House of Commons Act for an infraction of this section.
The hon. member has attempted to anticipate any objections that might be raised and to provide immunity from the penalty provided under another statute. It seems to me that the terms of the bill are within the scope of the kind of legislation that can be sponsored by private members of the House.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ALLOW MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT TO PARTICIPATE IN DELIBERATIONS OF CROWN AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the point made by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) when he suggested that this bill should be regarded as in order because the money that would be paid to a Member of Parliament under the bill would not be new money. He argued that it is money that is already provided in a statute, and therefore it is not an additional charge upon the treasury. I am afraid I have to remind him that the rules in this respect do not stop at that point. For example, citation 246(3) of Beau-chesne's Fourth Edition, which is one of the citations that bear on this point, reads as follows:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the Crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the Crown has demanded or recommended a charge.
The rest of the sentence states that this applies to ministers as well as to private members. The hon. member for Cochrane argued that his bill does not involve any new money, but it seems to me that he is in effect seeking to amend two statutes. One is the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, which has already laid down the conditions under which money is to be spent, and one of those conditions is the paying of expenses of certain identified people. He changes that condition by adding a Member of Parliament as a person who can be one of these people. The other act that he is seeking to amend is the Senate and House of Commons Act, and perhaps some other legislation affecting us, which says that Members of Parliament cannot get money in this way.
I concede the right of Parliament to pass a bill that would alter that condition, but since it is altering the financial situation in respect of Members of Parliament I submit that it would require the royal recommendation. In other words, it seems to me that on two counts this
Canadian Commercial Corporation Act bill offends the principle that I just read from Beau-chesne that a proposal infringes the financial initiative of the Crown, not only by increasing the amount of money involved but by extending its objects and purposes or relaxing the conditions and qualifications which have been expressed in a royal recommendation. On these counts it seems to me that the argument that it is not new money must fall to the ground.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the point of view put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with respect to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) in terms of the bill not seeking to provide an expenditure of additional moneys. I submit that the word "additional" has no place in the consideration of whether the bill is in order in accordance with Standing Order 62(1). Your predecessors, Sir, have always been very precise and careful in interpreting Standing Order 62(1) in its broadest possible sense and, as I recall it, Mr. Speaker-when there has been any indication in a bill regarding the expenditure of what is looked upon as public revenue-has always used that to say that the bill should founder on that point. Standing Order 62 provides:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue-
It is not a matter of any additional part, or anything that has not already been committed; this is a bill that seeks to appropriate some part of the public revenue to pay salary and expenses to a Member of Parliament who may sit on the Canadian Commercial Corporation. For my part, I have always felt that there should be a more lax approach taken by Mr. Speaker and the House in this respect, because I think there is far too much rigidity which generally has impinged upon the desires of hon. members to bring ideas forward.
I am very interested in seeing this bill proceed so that we will be able to examine the concept whereby it is suggested that one group of politicians, namely, the government, should have the right to appoint some other politicians to a corporation such as this. There are a number of other bills on the order paper along this line. This principle should be examined with some care and I suggest, Sir, that if you find after argument that the bill does founder and does not meet the test demanded by Standing Order 62(1), perhaps the hon. member could ask the unanimous consent of the House-the House is its own master in this regard-to waive Standing Order 62 in order that the bill may be proceeded with and considered.
I think the proposal in the bill is one that should be carefully examined in full public light in order to see what other manoeuvring might be involved in this system of allowing the government to appointment its friends to particular boards and corporations.

speechtext: I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if this bill could stand and retain its place so that it would be in the same position as the other bill with which we dealt.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the progress we have made in this hour, and in view of the unexpected moving along of the order of business, I wonder if we might call it five o'clock.

Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in light of the fact that, spurred by the opposition, this House has made tremendous progress today, could somebody on the other side please indicate the business for Monday? I presume we will go back to the tax appeal board. But assuming the House makes the same disposition of this matter as it has with the other bills, could some kind soul on the government side indicate what business will follow on Monday, in the way of any change in the order of business as announced by the President of the Privy Council on Thursday? We have already dealt with the business indicated by him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, we have not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that Bill C-174 will be before the House on Monday, respecting the tax review board.
On motion of Mr. Mahoney the House adjourned at 4.38 p.m.
